title: Need advice - AI art generation
author: Equivalent-Hippo9905
selftext:
Hi, I am completely new to game development. It has been a journey over the past month learning about different terms and getting my game in shape. I am doing this part time since I work with AI a lot at my job, and as the capabilities got better, I wanted to apply it to my hobby. 

Ran into a big problem with the art asset. I have minimal experience with Blender and Godot, and I am terrible at artwork. So I wanted to use Claude with Blender and Godot MCP to help with creating them. But they are always not up to my standard.

It seems to work for pixel art and I see a lot of AI art generator doing that but what about more realistic type of 2D art? Online seems to call the style I am looking for as painterly or painted ink. 

Any advice will be appreciated!

comments.author: Rsouss
comments.body: Take your art example: a character, create an AI video with the movements you want, and then capture the frames from the video.

replies.author: Equivalent-Hippo9905
replies.body: Any tools that you have used successfully for this?

replies.author: Rsouss
replies.body: Yes, you can generate the video in King AI. To capture the frames, I have my own tool that I created. However, it's very simple to use. To capture the frames correctly, set the timer to 0.2 milliseconds to capture the video, and reduce the video speed to 0.50x.

comments.author: bettertagsweretaken
comments.body: Meshy and 3D AI Studio provide excellent image to mesh quality. Incredibly high poly count, though. And you still have to rig and animate it. Mixamo is free on that front, but it's a pipeline I'm not familiar with. I'm doing a game with minimal animations where VFX carry all the animation.

replies.author: Equivalent-Hippo9905
replies.body:
Thanks for the tips. I am also doing a game now with minimal animations (perhaps even none) and just using VFX but what about background art and the character art itself? I am finding it hard to get those looking good.

And for VFX any tools that you rely on?

replies.author: bettertagsweretaken
replies.body:
I'm building everything in Godot and between me, Claude, and Fable/Opus we're building out the particles. 

I have to say, the VFX systems were the ones that required me to get my hands dirtiest. I know how and why each setting in the particle systems works! That being said, Claude can and has authored some art that was almost passable on first blush. 

For the background art and stuff you need to find an output that will repair produce the same results and then generate multiple images of the target in multiple angles (for characters).

For background art, I'm lucky again, i guess. I use the art from the game itself (like the actual in-game levels as screenshots and background materials), because it's a tactics game. Anything i generate for it would be an abstraction and that's not helpful for showing people the game itself.

replies.author: Equivalent-Hippo9905
replies.body: Thanks! I will give it a go! Wish you success in your game too!

comments.author: Ok-Lengthiness-6692
comments.body: Send chatgpt some images of the style you like, ask for it to describe it for a new prompt. Then use that prompt and the source images to generate the art you want. Collect dozens of new examples you have generated and use those as references to generate more art.

replies.author: Equivalent-Hippo9905
replies.body:
I tried that and it seems to be able to analyse but it hasn't been very effective in re-creating the chatgpt mockup looks. 

Do I need to teach it anything for how to use blender etc? I fed it the blender official documentation and it got better but still not up to par

replies.author: Ok-Lengthiness-6692
replies.body: I'm not sure I understand what exactly you are trying to do. You said 2D art, but are using blender. Are there any examples of games you are trying to replicate? Or what is the goal exactly here. Blender is generally a 3D tool.

replies.author: Equivalent-Hippo9905
replies.body: I am doing them as 2D but I am not sure what is the best tool. Was researching online and the recommendation that I got was that blender is effective at creating 2D from 3D asset. So i went with that method. Should I be using something else?

replies.author: Ok-Lengthiness-6692
replies.body: Ohh are you trying to create 2D spritesheets from 3D models? Like diablo 2 style?

replies.author: Equivalent-Hippo9905
replies.body: Yup. At the same time, I am trying out ideas such as a more 3D background and seeing how it feels

replies.author: Ok-Lengthiness-6692
replies.body: Ok that makes much more sense. Yes you can have AI write a plugin for blender to create 8, 16 or 32 directional spritesheets for your game. I have done all this several times before. Just ask the AI how to do this step by step, if you don't understand a step, ask for clarification. Do not rush anything. You will figure it out. The biggest bottleneck I discovered was animating certain models, but there are platforms like mixamo that allow you to do this somewhat easily.

comments.author: Some-Mistake8113
comments.body: I have Meshy generate my assets, then I have it do a headless blender pass on the original glb output, decimating it to a tri budget after repairing the asset (flipped normals, welding holes, aligning tris that are messed up, etc). I have found that it’s actually better to decimate with this repair process in blender instead of using the Remesh Meshy feature; which can create even more defects. Also, I’ve learned there’s a big difference between textures that are tiled in blender and atlas textures built through Meshy- the more complicated the asset and the bigger the asset- the higher I crank the texture resolution because the textures wrap around the whole object, while in blender they can tile with materials you make instead of wrapping around the whole object. Not sure if I used the right terminology there.

replies.author: Equivalent-Hippo9905
replies.body: That's interesting. I will give it a go.  Are there any issues that you hit while doing this?

replies.author: Some-Mistake8113
replies.body: Foliage like trees and plants are better made in blender. You can have it make the bark material and derive the PBR materials. Base albedo should be a seamless tileable square image you can make with ChatGPT. For leaves you can use leaf cards and apply them to the branches. Best result I’ve found for trees and plants. Meshy will not do good with any foliage, but it’s great at regular items if you do a repair pass in blender.

comments.author: CycleMother2006
comments.body:
GPT Image 2.0 can produce great painterly art. For something local try Krea 2. No licensing fees for commercial use  unless you start making over 1 mil / year. Those can cover you for any 2d. Animations you'd still need to do those by hand or work in a img2vid frame extraction workflow and settle for the poor quality that entails. 

I do animations in Spine 2D, though there are free alternatives that, while not as comprehensive, can still support the animation range most people would need (Dragonbones for one, and most engines have some level of rigged animation support.)

You shouldn't have a problem producing assets in the painterly style. Although animating them is trickier. Rigged animation is harder the more detail you add into something generally, because it's harder to find good places to slice up the image and dramatic animations with the image can lead to distortions that you don't see with simpler styles. img2vid works alright for the style, but you'll have to accept that frame by frame it's going to look pretty bad, and relies heavily on the blurring of a lot of frames together to maintain sensibility (so you're never getting away with lower frame animations. So depending on the size of your assets, animation data size can get quite large when pushing 24-30 FPS and a walk cycle ends up being like 50 frames. You're either forced to have smaller sprites (so be careful of zoom) or massive file bloat. That being said, I haven't personally worked with a painterly style for rigged animation, so maybe it's easier than I'm giving it credit for. I don't generally see those games use it though. The closest you get is games like Chaos Zero Nightmare where the detailed anime sprites use it for idles (but they use a much simpler style for their more active animated sprites). Unicorn Overlord is another one that gets ose, but is still more cel-shaded than not, even if it can feel painterly at times. And they did chop their sprites up into like 50 layers. Plus the sprites themselves are less painterly than the background itself.

One thing you could consider, depending on what the painted ink style you actually want to make is like... Is consider a more flat color pipeline for generation and then have AI help you produce a shader that can translate those flat color shapes into painted ink. This is how a lot of games with extreme styles maintain consistency. :It's also just tremendously easier to hire artists to make art in simpler styles that are easier to manipulate for things like animation, and then have shaders handle the heavy lifting to give it the appearance you want. I mean that's basically how 99% of cel-shaded games have worked, and stylized games in general, and when you see them without their shaders / tonemapping / etc running, you're like,  "This game looks like garbage", but drool over the aesthetics when everything is in place.

comments.author: Game2Entertainment
comments.body:
Based on my previous experience with a similar problem (using Gemini), here is my thinking:  
1. Breaking down your workflow into smaller steps instead of trying to solve everything at once.   
For example, your task should be: 3d model → x → y ....... → final 2d.  
2. Consider instruction following: give the LLM a clear step-by-step workflow instead of only a final prompt. Then iteratively tune each step based on the output.  
3. Since your game probably needs a consistent art style, I wouldn't optimize each image individually. Build a pipeline that produces "good enough" results first (e.g., 70/100 quality), then optimize the pipeline itself so most assets fit your style.  
Methods:  
A. give reference images (few-shot-style guidance): provide examples of the target style.  
B. find style keywords ("magic words"): terms like painterly or painted ink can influence results, but require experimentation.  
C. refinement pipeline: generate a solid base first, then use algorithms or tools to improve consistency and quality. DO NOT dream that everything can be done at production quality with a single prompt.
